Chapter 4: Redefining Identity — Living Beyond Labels
When illness or disability steps into your life, it can bring along a stack of labels—patient, client, disabled, chronically ill. On the surface, these words are just meant to describe. But, often, they end up feeling more like cages than anything else.
Have you ever noticed how quickly the world narrows its gaze? Sometimes, all people see is the wheelchair, the cane, or a medical chart. But deep down, the real person is still there—the same dreams, the same quirks, and that same stubborn hope that refuses to go away.
Think about this: there was a teenager, once known for her quick wit and her love of sports. Suddenly, she found herself introduced as "the girl with the rare disease." Her friends and teachers meant well, but the label just stuck. She started to notice little changes—people speaking more slowly, offering help she didn’t need, or sometimes even avoiding her completely. At first, she tried to fit into that new role, shrinking back from her passions and letting others decide who she was. But after a while, the discomfort just built up.
One afternoon, while she watched her friends play basketball, it finally hit her: she missed being seen for who she truly was, not just what she “had.”
Most of us don’t realize how quickly identity can shrink. The world’s expectations kind of seep in, and before you know it, you’re tempted to accept a smaller version of yourself. But here’s the thing—identity is stubborn. It doesn’t just go quietly. It pushes back, wanting to be recognized. For so many people, the journey really becomes about reclaiming old passions, discovering new ones, and refusing to let a diagnosis do all the defining.
Take, for example, a man who’d spent years building his career in finance. Suddenly, a neurological condition forced him to step away from work. And with that loss of work, it felt like he’d lost himself, too. Months went by, and he just drifted, unsure of his place in the world. Then, a chance conversation with a neighbor—someone who just needed some budgeting advice—reminded him of what he was good at. Slowly, he started volunteering, running financial workshops at the local community center. Sure, the work was different, but that sense of purpose? It came right back. He realized that, even though his circumstances had changed, his core identity was still his.
Redefining identity isn’t about pretending reality doesn’t exist. It’s about weaving together new experiences, finding ways to honor both the things you’ve lost and the things you’ve gained. For some, that means jumping into advocacy, using your story to help others. For others, it’s about quiet persistence, just showing up every day and refusing to fade into the background.
Over time, those labels? They start to lose their grip. The world might still see the wheelchair or the medical chart, but inside, you know exactly who you are. The real fight isn’t just for health or independence—it’s for the right to be seen, fully and completely, without apology.
